title: Ask for the order
principle: Ask for the order. A "no" today often means "not yet".

screens.text: Remember Neil Rackham, the researcher from the last lesson? Many sellers think that closing lines, words that push a buyer to say yes now, help them sell more. But Rackham's team found that in big sales, such lines did not make buyers more likely to say yes.

screens.prompt: Why do you think pushing buyers to say yes did not help in big sales?

options.label: Big buyers feel pressure and need more time
Big buyers dislike talking about the price
Big buyers did not hear the price clearly

screens.why: Rackham's team found that pushing for a yes did not help in big sales. One possible reason is that big orders carry more risk for buyers. Pressure can make them pull away. In a small, quick sale, the risk is lower, so asking clearly is fine.

screens.title: The alternative-choice close
screens.text: In a small sale that is quick and has little risk, offer two ways to say yes. For example, "Monday or Tuesday?" This is called the alternative-choice close. But in a big sale with more risk, do not push. A buyer's "no" may mean "not yet".

screens.prompt: A family liked your cake at a party. Their son's birthday is next week. How should you ask for the order?

options.label: "Shall I send the full menu on WhatsApp?"
"Shall I take your order now, yes or no?"
"Shall I bring the cake Friday or Saturday?"

screens.why: Yes. Both choices mean the family will order. They only need to choose a day. They already liked your cake, and the birthday is soon. So it makes sense to ask clearly.

wrong.a: Sending the menu may help, but the family still has to decide what to do next. They are busy and may forget. They liked your cake, and the birthday is next week. Ask: "Friday or Saturday?"
wrong.b: Asking "yes or no" makes it easy to refuse. Instead, offer two days they can choose from: "Shall I bring it on Friday or Saturday?"

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Asking for an order matters in your bakery too. It is April, and wedding season has started. Families and wedding planners call to ask about cakes. Last year, many calls ended with "we'll let you know". But they never called you again.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six things buyers said. For each one, tell me: does the buyer mean no, or not yet?

items.text: "Ask me after I get my salary on the 1st."
"My husband decides. He comes back on Friday."
"Call me before Diwali. That is when we order."

screens.why: Good work. A real no means they do not need your cakes. Maybe they do not eat sweets, the event is cancelled, or they bake at home. "Not yet" means they are waiting for money, another person to decide, or the right time. Agree on a day to call again.

screens.prompt: A school principal says, "Not this term." Put these steps in order, with the first step at the top.
steps: Ask why she cannot order this term
Agree on a day to call her again
After the meeting, plan an offer for next term
Call her on that day with your offer
screens.why: Good work. First ask why she cannot order this term. Then agree on a day to call again. After the meeting, plan something useful for next term, like cakes for sports day. This gives you a reason to call.

screens.prompt: You asked a family, "Saturday or Sunday?" They said no because they had already ordered elsewhere. Was it wrong to ask?

options.label: Yes, because asking made them refuse
No, because asking made sense then
Yes, because waiting would be better

screens.why: Right. You learned this in Unit 1: judge a choice by what you knew when you made it. They liked your cake, and the date was close. So asking was right, even though they did not order.

wrong.a: They had already ordered elsewhere, so your question did not make them refuse. Remember Unit 1: judge your choice by what you knew then, not just what happened. Asking made sense.
wrong.c: Waiting would not change the fact that they had already ordered elsewhere. Remember Unit 1: judge your choice by what you knew then, not just what happened. Asking made sense.

screens.setup: It is late April. A wedding planner tried your cakes and liked them. She has weddings on 10 May and 17 May. Each needs a cake priced at ₹6,000, leaving you ₹3,000. This is a quick choice for her. She says, "Let me think."
screens.question: What do you say?

options.label: "Call me when you are ready to book."
options.outcome: You wait, but she does not call. On 12 May, you see photos of both weddings online. Another baker made the cakes. You lost the chance to earn ₹6,000 in profit.
options.why: She liked your cakes, and the wedding dates were close. But you did not ask her to book. Busy planners may book with the baker who asks first.
options.better: Ask which date she wants to book first. If she is not ready, agree on a day to talk again.

options.label: "Shall I book both dates or just 10 May?"
options.outcome: She smiles. "Book 10 May. For 17 May, the family is still deciding. Call me on Monday." You call on Monday, and she books that date too. You earn ₹6,000 from the two cakes.
options.why: You gave her two easy ways to say yes. She booked one cake. For the second, she was not ready yet. So you agreed on a day to call again instead of pushing her.

options.label: "Book both today and get ₹1,000 off each."
options.outcome: She books both cakes. But after the discount, you earn only ₹2,000 on each cake. That is ₹4,000 in total. Next time she books, she asks for the same discount.
options.why: You asked for the order, which was right. But you gave away ₹2,000 in discounts to make someone who already liked your cakes book sooner.
options.better: Ask which date she wants to book first. If she is not ready, agree on a day to talk again.

screens.text: In a small sale, ask for the ___ with two easy choices. When a buyer says "not yet", agree on a ___ to call again.
screens.why: Exactly. "Both dates, or just 10 May?" helped you get the first booking. Calling on Monday helped you get the second.

summary: Alternative-choice close: in a small sale, offer two easy ways to say yes to an order.
Pushing buyers to say yes does not help in big sales. In small sales, asking clearly can help.
When a buyer says no because of money, who decides, or timing, it may mean "not yet". Agree on a day to call again with something useful.

cards.front: A buyer liked your sample, and the event is next week. What should you say?
cards.back: Ask for the order by offering two easy choices that both mean yes.

cards.front: "My partner decides. He's back on Friday." What is this?
cards.back: Not yet. Agree on a day after Friday to call again.

cards.front: What did Rackham find about pushing for a yes in big sales?
cards.back: In big sales, pushing did not make buyers more likely to say yes. In a small sale, asking clearly is fine.

sources.label: Neil Rackham, SPIN Selling (Routledge, 1988): publisher's page
